source.title: Pretrained Diffusion Models for Unified Human Motion Synthesis
source.authors: Jian-Xin Ma; Shuai Bai; Chang Zhou

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper cites scaling laws as motivation for building a larger pretrained motion model, but its size comparison measures motion in-betweening metrics rather than testing power-law loss scaling, extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan et al. and reports a model-size ablation in Table 3. That ablation evaluates LaFAN1 motion in-betweening, not held-out language-model cross-entropy or a fitted power law. It does not test the claim versions. The table says L2P and NPSS follow the same trend as L2Q but gives no values for them.
record.test_reason: The paper cites Kaplan et al. only as motivation that larger models do better given enough data. Its only size comparison is a two-point ablation (50M vs 250M) on a downstream motion in-betweening metric (L2Q on LaFAN1). There is no loss sweep, no power-law fit, no extrapolation and no compute allocation. It neither tests nor relies on any version's quantitative form. The record's T4 is defensible but overstates the dependence: the paper does not use a scaling law as a tool.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors state that pretraining is vital for scaling model size without overfitting. The unpretrained 250M model is worse than the 50M model. The pretrained 250M model improves on it, matching at @5 and better at @15 and @30. They state that L2P and NPSS follow the same trend, without reporting values.
record.recipe_differences: A motion-generation model-size ablation using LaFAN1 in-betweening metrics, rather than language-model held-out loss sweeps and power-law fitting.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported effect changes with pretraining status and prediction horizon: the unpretrained 250M model scores worse than the 50M model at all three horizons; with pretraining, scores are equal at @5 and lower at @15 and @30.

fits_no_version.finding: Going from 50M to 250M in a motion diffusion model worsens LaFAN1 L2Q without pretraining. With pretraining it is equal at @5 and slightly better at @15 and @30.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In data-scarce motion synthesis, larger models help on downstream metrics only when pretrained on a larger combined corpus; otherwise they overfit.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says source code and checkpoints will be released before publication.
record.problems: The model-size comparison reports only two sizes. The reported outcome is a downstream motion metric, not a loss-scaling fit; no uncertainty estimates are stated. L2P and NPSS are said to follow the same trend, but their values are not provided.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows retained. Table 3 says L2P and NPSS follow the same trend as L2Q but does not report their values.

untested.parts: No held-out loss measured across sizes, tokens or compute.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
Motion-diffusion modality, but only two sizes on a downstream metric; no power-law form examined.
Two sizes only; no predictability relation to scale or loss.

record.verdict_notes: Changed the relation to cites_only/T6, since Kaplan et al. appears only as motivating background (ref [18], intro). The rows record a genuine but off-claim ablation; they are kept with versions none and their states set to cannot_determine relative to the claim versions.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No fits on small runs or predictions of larger-run loss.
No fixed-compute allocation comparison or parameter/token scaling trend.
No comparison of architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Although the study concerns human motion, it does not test whether power-law loss scaling holds in another modality or training regime.
No test of downstream performance predictability from pretraining loss or a scaling law.
No analysis of fitted exponents, fitting choices, or bending power-law curves.
